groups.instructions: Read the article about classroom sound and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
A teacher moved a weekly discussion from a carpeted room to a larger one with bare walls. She expected the extra space to help. Instead, students at the back asked speakers to repeat themselves more often, and some who had spoken regularly stopped taking part. The front row could hear the teacher well enough, which made the problem easy to miss.

The building was not especially noisy. The difficulty came from sound returning from hard surfaces. When reflected sound reaches a listener a little after the direct sound, it can blur the boundary between one syllable and the next. Raising one's voice makes both the direct sound and the reflections louder. In a room like this, speaking more loudly may make words no easier to separate.

To investigate, students recorded the same short announcement in both rooms. They kept the speaker and microphone in similar positions and asked a separate class to write down what it heard. Listeners missed more words in the recording from the larger room. A second recording there was made after thick fabric was hung on two walls. The missed-word count fell, although the larger room still did not match the carpeted one.

The teacher kept the fabric and began arranging seats in a broad semicircle. She also changed how her students took turns, leaving a short gap after each speaker. She explained that the exercise had uncovered a barrier to participation: students may follow a single familiar voice well enough while struggling to follow several voices from different directions. The number of people a room can seat says very little about how well those people will hear one another.

questions.question_text: Which students first showed signs of difficulty hearing?

options.text: The pupils closest to the teacher.
Visitors from the class that listened to recordings.

questions.question_text: What does “blur” suggest in paragraph two?

options.text: Make the gap between words longer.
Make the sound less loud in every seat.

questions.question_text: Why might speaking more loudly fail to solve the problem?

options.text: The direct sound becomes weaker as volume increases.
The person speaking starts to use fewer syllables.
The unwanted reflections get louder as well.
The back row receives only direct sound.

questions.question_text: What did the separate class do?

options.text: Write down the announcement it heard.
Read the announcement for both recordings.
Decide which fabric to hang on the walls.

questions.question_text: Why were the speaker and microphone put in similar positions in both rooms?

options.text: To reduce differences due to the recording setup.
To increase the number of reflections in both rooms equally.
To help the speaker remember the sentences without a script.
To keep students from knowing which voice they heard.

questions.question_text: Which statement accurately compares the room after the fabric was added with the carpeted room?

options.text: The fabric made the larger room as clear as the carpeted room.
The two rooms had identical scores before the fabric was added.
The fabric improved only the recording in the carpeted room.
The fabric helped, but listeners still performed better with the carpeted room recording.

questions.question_text: Why might a short gap between speakers help?

options.text: It ensures that all contributions come from the same direction.
It forces students to speak loudly enough to cover reflections.
It gives the previous voice less opportunity to overlap with the next one.
It means the teacher can replace unfamiliar voices with her own.

questions.question_text: What does “those people” near the end refer to?

options.text: The teachers who moved the discussion.
The people a room can hold.
The speakers who made the recordings.

questions.question_text: Which option best restates the last sentence?

options.text: The more people in a room, the easier it is for them to hear each other.
Seating capacity alone tells us little about how easily people can hear each other.
A room that seats fewer people always has better acoustics.
Rooms with fixed seats are unsuitable for any discussion.

questions.question_text: What is the article mainly about?

options.text: How to increase the audience size for a classroom event.
Why a teacher stopped recording spoken announcements at school.
Why written instructions are always better than spoken ones.
How the sound of a room can affect participation and how a class investigated it.

groups.instructions: Read the article on a stationery exchange and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
The council at a secondary school set out a tray of spare pens and notebooks next to the reception desk. It was intended for students who arrived without supplies. At first, students rarely took anything. Some later told a tutor that taking a pen felt like making an announcement in the busiest part of the school. They did not want to explain why they needed one.

The council tried a second location beside the classroom cupboards. It also changed the wording on the sign. Instead of “Supplies for students in need,” the notice read “Take what you will use. Leave what you can spare.” Several pupils brought erasers or loose sheets. The council drew on those contributions and added basic items from its budget whenever the tray ran low. Students who never left an item were welcome to take one.

As more supplies went out, the treasurer worried that the scheme was encouraging waste. A teacher suggested checking what students actually did with the items. At the end of a week, tutors asked classes to estimate how often the supplies had helped them start work on time. They also noted unopened items left in classrooms. A tally of items taken would not distinguish between an extra pen in a forgotten drawer and a pen used immediately in a lesson. Few sealed items remained at the end of the week, and the students gave several examples of work they could start without borrowing from classmates.

The council kept the tray and added a second one in a part of the building without classroom cupboards. Before doing so, it asked pupils which locations would feel ordinary to visit. The aim was to make taking a pencil look like any other step in preparing for a lesson.

questions.question_text: Why did some students avoid the first tray?

options.text: They thought the supplies belonged to reception staff.
They were told to leave notebooks where they found them.
They did not know the desk was open during lessons.
Taking something there felt too public.

questions.question_text: What change in message did the new sign make?

options.text: It asked each visitor to prove that they had forgotten an item.
It treated taking and sharing supplies as ordinary actions available to students.
It suggested only people with spare supplies should visit.
It made borrowing an official task supervised by reception.

questions.question_text: What did the council do when supplies ran low?

options.text: It bought basic items using its budget.
It closed the tray until every student contributed.
It returned the remaining items to reception.
It asked tutors to lend their own stationery during class.

questions.question_text: What does “drew on” mean in the second paragraph?

options.text: Used as a source of supplies.
Returned to the people who donated.

questions.question_text: Why was the treasurer concerned?

options.text: A rise in items taken might not mean that more items were useful.
Spending on notebooks had already exceeded the budget.
Donations had replaced every type of item bought by the school.
Students were borrowing items from reception without returning them.

questions.question_text: What could the teachers' reports show that a tally of items taken could not?

options.text: Which kinds of stationery cost the most to replace.
Whether the items helped pupils begin classroom work.
How many students saw the original sign at reception.
What fraction of students contributed to the scheme.

questions.question_text: Which two kinds of information did the tutors gather?

options.text: Pupils' reports about starting work and notes on unopened items left in classrooms.
Reception visits and names of pupils needing replacement pens.
The number of donors and the cost of replacing each eraser.
Classroom cupboard space and the number of pupils absent each day.

questions.question_text: How did pupils contribute to selecting a site for the extra tray?

options.text: They were told to select the busiest public spot.
They voted on whether to return the main tray to reception.
They were asked where visiting a tray would feel normal.
They reported which rooms contained the largest cupboards.

questions.question_text: What does “doing so” in the final paragraph refer to?

options.text: Retaining the tray beside the original reception desk.
Asking pupils to bring more erasers.
Adding an extra tray elsewhere in the building.
Recording whether pupils opened the items.

questions.question_text: Which title best matches the article?

options.text: A School Exchange Designed Around What Pupils Actually Need.
Why Students Should Buy Their Own School Supplies.
Making Reception the Only Place to Get Spare Stationery.
How Counting Pens Can Replace Student Feedback.
